The suggested citation for this guideline is: Infant feeding in areas of Zika virus transmission. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2016. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations to guide governments, ministries of health, policymakers, and healthcare workers in regions affected by Zika virus transmission. It aims to assist in the development of local and national protocols and policies on infant feeding, including breastfeeding practices, in areas of Zika virus transmission and their implementation. It may also be used to inform communication with the general public. Zika virus is a mosquito-borne virus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, which also transmit other vector-borne diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. Currently, there is no treatment or vaccine specifically available to protect against Zika virus infection. This guideline is part of a body of work exploring available evidence for possible acceptable medical reasons for temporary or long-term cessation of breastfeeding. It updates the interim guidance on breastfeeding in the context of the Zika virus published by WHO on 25 February 2016. This guideline was developed in response to a Public Health Emergency of International Concern and followed a rapid advice framework to produce timely guidance. The process adhered to the basic steps for guideline development outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development, with time modifications to meet the urgent need for advice. The steps included identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations (including research priorities), and planning for dissemination, implementation, equity and ethical considerations, and impact evaluation and updating of the guideline. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to prepare evidence profiles related to preselected topics based on up-to-date systematic reviews. A guideline development group meeting on the Zika virus outbreak was held on 17–19 March 2016 in Geneva, Switzerland. The group included experts in infant feeding, nutrition surveillance, nutrition in emergencies, pediatrics, and infectious diseases (virology and risk assessment). During the meeting, the group discussed the balance of consequences of breastfeeding or consuming breast milk from a mother infected with Zika virus and finalized the recommendation. Five experts served as technical peer reviewers of the draft guideline. This publication is a World Health Organization (WHO) guideline. A WHO guideline is any document containing WHO recommendations about health interventions, whether clinical, public health, or policy-related. A recommendation provides information about what policymakers, healthcare providers, or patients should do, implying a choice between different interventions that impact health and resource use. This WHO guideline has been approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The systematic review identified two case reports describing three mother–infant pairs. All three breastfeeding mothers had confirmed Zika virus infection and were symptomatic within three days of delivery. Two of the three infants born to these mothers had confirmed Zika virus infection. The Zika virus was detected in the breast milk of all three mothers, and replicative virus was shown in cell culture in samples from one mother. However, the current data are insufficient to conclude transmission via breastfeeding. The systematic review also identified three surveys confirming the presence of the Zika virus in serum and saliva of adult women and men. No studies have investigated the presence of Zika virus in sweat. The overall quality of evidence for suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection among infants or young children breastfeeding from mothers with Zika virus infection, and the presence of Zika virus in breast milk, was very low. The recommendation is that infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, or who reside in or have traveled to areas of ongoing Zika virus transmission, should be fed according to normal infant feeding guidelines. They should start breastfeeding within one hour of birth, be exclusively breastfed for six months, and have timely introduction of adequate, safe, and properly fed complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding up to two years of age or beyond. Mothers who decide to breastfeed should receive skilled support from healthcare workers to initiate and sustain breastfeeding, whether they or their infants have suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection. Infants with congenital anomalies (e.g., microcephaly) or those presenting with feeding difficulties should be supported to breastfeed. Skilled feeding support from health professionals, including breastfeeding support, should be provided. This is a strong recommendation, meaning the guideline development group is confident that the desirable effects of breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus transmission outweigh the undesirable effects. Families and communities play a central role in supporting optimal infant and young child feeding and improving infant health. Properly trained and supported community cadres can provide counseling, practical breastfeeding support, problem-solving, and interactive peer sessions. Multidisciplinary teams may be necessary for infants requiring specialist support in infant feeding, particularly those with congenital anomalies or breastfeeding difficulties. The guideline development group highlighted the limited evidence available on the risk of Zika virus transmissibility through breastfeeding. Further research findings may impact the guidance on infant feeding in areas of Zika virus transmission. The WHO steering group will continue to monitor research developments in this area and review new data within six months of publication to determine whether an update is needed. If an update is warranted, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the process following formal WHO procedures.
